extracted.subtask_description: Practical rules and organizational principles for running a common school: reducing interruptions, dividing time, conducting recitations, delegating duties, and governing pupil behavior. Emphasizes concrete procedures (e.g., 'Study Card'), schedules, and how/when to delegate to students while retaining teacher authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whispering limited to prescribed times ('Study Card')
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt the principle of 'whispering at limited and prescribed times alone' using a visible signal (the 'Study Card') to indicate when speaking is permitted or forbidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: hang a Study Card (board/plate) visible to the class; when up, pupils must not speak except for extraordinary occurrences (sickness, sending a message, etc.); at the close of each half hour a bell is struck and card taken down. Use pleasant tone and make the rule a joint 'experiment' rather than a punitive confession. The chief point is to secure the principle; apparatus construction may vary (simple pasteboard card to gilded tin plate with pulley and bell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw a precise line; avoid ad hoc exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Make rules with a 'precise line' so that exceptions are not routinely made; individuals must submit to occasional inconvenience to promote the general good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale/example: a single apparent exception (e.g., a pupil going to fetch a book) invites others to claim exceptions on progressively slighter grounds until the rule is disregarded. Therefore rules must be framed and enforced in ways that resist gradual erosion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use voluntary public reporting to encourage honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Solicit voluntary reports of rule transgressions from pupils (standing/sitting method) to habituate honest self-accounting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: at day's end ask all to rise; allow those unwilling or unable to report to sit. Call for counts by levels of transgression (once, 2–4 times, etc.). After reports, praise honesty and frame the exercise as an 'experiment' so it is not a reluctant confession. Acknowledge likely dishonest reports and plan to repeat and follow up next day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignore deliberate opponents; secure a working majority
rubrics_metrics.description: If some pupils refuse participation merely to thwart, take no notice of them; obtain and show a great majority in favor so opposition seems inconsequential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychology: when pupils see opposition ignored they become ashamed of obstructive behavior; securing a visible majority encourages cooperation and diminishes the influence of contrarians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a visible signaling apparatus to mark study/rest times
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ a physical device (board/plate, cord, pulley, bell) to mark and announce the transitions between study and rest periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction details given (tin/brass plate hinged on board, cord over pulley with tassel as counterpoise, clapper touching bell). Variations are acceptable; the important point is clarity of signal. Even a crude pasteboard card and table bell sufficed in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign a specific time for mending pens or delegate the task
rubrics_metrics.description: Mending pens should have a specific time assigned rather than interrupting classes repeatedly; preferably do not mend pens yourself but delegate to trained older pupils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options: teacher may mend at home, set aside a special time, or teach four or five older/more intelligent students to mend many pens daily and apportion scholars among them so teacher is relieved entirely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize individual interruptions; teach 'in masses'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid frequent private assistance; teach the class as a whole when possible because time per pupil is limited (estimate: 2–4 minutes each).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before assigning a lesson, anticipate difficulties and tell them to the whole class; direct how pupils should act in likely emergencies; ask pupils to bring unforeseen difficulties to the next recitation so one explanation serves many. Use class-time to answer shared problems rather than repeating answers individually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not answer questions about where or what the lesson is
rubrics_metrics.description: Refuse inquiries about the location or extent of assigned lessons (e.g., 'Where is the next lesson?'), forcing pupils to remember or consult classmates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample dialogue shows how to decline pleasantly: reply that you do not remember and that it is their responsibility; direct them to ask a classmate when appropriate (e.g., when Study Card is down). The rule discourages dependency and repeated interruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve uninterrupted attention during recitations
rubrics_metrics.description: When presiding at a class, the teacher's attention must be undisturbed and devoted exclusively to instructing; recitations are central to teaching and require full attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt other tasks while hearing recitations. Each recitation should have a specified time adhered to strictly. The teacher should aim to instruct, enlarge ideas, and awaken interest, so arrangements should permit exclusive attention to the class while it is engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify and enforce precise recitation times and transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Each recitation should have its specified time and transitions should be signaled (bell) and rigidly observed to maintain discipline and system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps: divide forenoon/afternoon into subject blocks (diagram provided), ring a bell five minutes before the half-hour and exactly at its close, appoint an officer/pupil to ring, allow short rests at designated times so classes change promptly and regularly. Teacher example: put bell in a pupil's hands to show teacher also conforms to system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare and post a precise daily schedule (diagram)
rubrics_metrics.description: Display a clear diagram showing the division of time and class assignments (subjects per half-hour), including marks for recesses (R) and General exercise (G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have older scholars draw a large sheet to paste up; insert class names under respective heads. The posted plan communicates that arrangements are systematic and applies equally to teacher and pupils, aiding regularity and cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use General Exercise periods for whole-school instruction and business
rubrics_metrics.description: Set aside 'General exercise' periods for matters affecting the whole school: group studies (punctuation, spelling), cases of discipline, general directions, and familiar lectures/questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: two short daily periods—one for the 'business of the school' (discipline, arrangements), the other for lectures or studies profitably attended to by the whole school. Many important matters are best handled at such times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher as absolute monarch with delegated pupil responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: School government should be a 'monarchy'—the teacher possessing exclusive power—combined with free and continual delegation of power to pupils within limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegate as much business as possible so pupils are trained to manage affairs and take interest, but make clear that this is delegated power which the teacher can revoke. Responsibility remains with the teacher and delegation should increase according to pupils' ability to bear trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce self-government gradually; select capable delegates
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare pupils gradually for delegated duties; begin with small, concrete tasks (e.g., distributing books) and select pleasant, popular, reliable pupils as officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not announce grand designs; test cooperation with simple experiments (appoint four distributors, one per division). Proper initial selection and gradual assumption of duties help secure popularity and success of delegated tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about full republican self-government
rubrics_metrics.description: Real self-government (entire surrender of management to pupils) is hazardous and often fails unless under exceptionally favorable conditions and with a teacher who can still exercise effective leadership ('generalship').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case study: Gardiner Lyceum's experiment showed early successes but later problems (trial manipulation, acquittals, need for adult intervention). Such plans may succeed briefly but are often eventually abandoned; teachers should limit and supervise student government carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect approximation, not perfection; follow up persistent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not expect universal obedience or perfect operation of plans; aim for approximation to excellence and employ follow-up measures for those who will not yield to initial inducements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical realism: unprincipled or deceiving characters will remain; proper treatment may reform them but new similar characters will appear. Use additional measures after a few days for persistent offenders; initial voluntary measures are intended to secure as large a majority as possible.
